Subject: Subprocessor flow-down: change notices & subcontract approvals (MSA redlines)

Hi Maya —

Thanks for sending the Order Form draft this morning. We reviewed the MSA redlines attached to your package and have a couple of follow ups specifically around the subprocessor and vendor flow-down clauses:

- Change notice timing: your redline asks for a 30-day prior notice for any new subprocessor onboarding plus an approval right. We usually provide change notices but cannot commit to a prior approval that would block onboarding. Could you confirm if a 30-day notice with the option to object (with a defined remediation/mitigation path) would suffice for FinApps?

- Subcontracting approvals: the MSA currently requires Redwood to obtain written consent for any subcontractor that processes customer data. We can commit to a pre-approved subprocessor list and notice + objection flow for new subprocessors; however, blanket consent for all levels of subcontracting is operationally difficult. Would a tiered approach be acceptable (pre-approved list + short notice for downstream subcontractors)?

- DPA/flow-down: we attach an updated DPA excerpt with clarifying language around data segregation and notification timelines. Please see RWD_MSA_redline_v3.pdf attached.

I’m looping in Priyom to confirm commercial impact and Laura (legal) separately — she’ll get a full redline shortly. Goal: get to a mutually acceptable compromise that keeps your auditors comfortable while not blocking our infra ops cadence.

Would you be available for a short call tomorrow to resolve the open bullets?

Thanks,
Marcus
Senior Sales Manager
Redwood Inference

Attachments: RWD_MSA_redline_v3.pdf
From: Maya Reynolds <m.reynolds@finapps.com>

Cc: FinApps Procurement <procurement@finapps.com>, Emily Santos <emily.santos@lawpartners.com>
Date: Tue, 10 Feb 2026 11:05:00 -08:00
Subject: Re: Subprocessor flow-down: change notices & subcontract approvals (MSA redlines)

Marcus — thanks for the quick reply and the draft. A couple of clarifications from our side before a call:

1) Approvals vs objection: our security team insists on the ability to withhold approval for any subprocessor that materially increases risk (e.g., changes jurisdiction or introduces new technology with unclear controls). An objection-only model without the right to stop onboarding isn’t sufficient for us.

2) Scope of "subcontractor": we define subcontractor broadly (any downstream provider engaged by Redwood or its subprocessors). We need clear flow-down of security obligations to the final-handlers.

3) Change notice windows: 30 days is fine, but we’d like to preserve a 3-week window to submit any compliance-related questions and potentially request a hold while we validate controls.

Attached are our annotated comments (FinApps_OrderForm_comments.docx). Emily — can you review the specific flow-down language (see p.4) and advise whether the approval vs objection split is workable with a gating clause for material risk?

If you’re ok, let’s move the call to Thursday 10:30am PT so we have Laura on as well.

Best,
Maya
VP, Procurement & Security
FinApps

Attachments: FinApps_OrderForm_comments.docx
From: Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.inference.com>

Date: Tue, 10 Feb 2026 14:18:00 -08:00
Subject: Fwd: Subprocessor flow-down: change notices & subcontract approvals (MSA redlines)

Folks — forwarding Maya’s comments. Quick notes from Legal:

- We should avoid any language that gives the customer unilateral veto over routine infra subprocessors (e.g., logging, monitoring) because that would prevent us from operating the service.

- Proposed compromise: 1) maintain a pre-approved subprocessor list in Schedule X (we’ve attached a draft table, RWD_Subprocessor_Table.xlsx); 2) 30-day notice for new subprocessors; 3) allow customer to raise a written objection within 14 days of notice on the basis of documented material risk; 4) if objection is raised, parties must engage in a 30-day remediation/mitigation process; 5) if unresolved after remediation, the customer can seek limited remedies (e.g., temporary suspension for that dataset but not wholesale termination of the MSA).

- On the DPA front: we must ensure any flow-down obligations are materially equivalent but cannot include terms that force us to disclose vendor source code or internal control docs beyond standard SOC2/attestation artifacts.

I’ll attend the Thursday slot and bring suggested redline text. I think this language balances operational needs with their audit requirements.

Laura Bennett
Deputy General Counsel
Redwood Inference

Quick commercial notes:

- If we concede to a customer approval right for any material-risk subprocessor, we should add an SLA-based compensatory credit if they exercise a hold that impacts throughput. That keeps commercial balance.

- Also recommend we limit the definition of "material risk" to a narrow set (jurisdiction change outside of US/EU, introduction of a subprocessor that stores unencrypted customer data, or use of a subprocessor in a high-risk jurisdiction).

- I can offer FinApps a 5% credit on committed spend for the first 6 months once terms are agreed to offset perceived risk; let me know if Legal wants that in the Order Form.

Priyom

Thanks all for the notes and the table. The call was helpful — Emily and I walked through the proposed remediation path and timeline and that should work for our security team provided:

- The 14-day objection window is preserved and is counted from the notice email timestamp.
- If remediation fails, FinApps can request a temporary suspension for the impacted workload for up to 60 days while we validate controls.
- We need explicit DPA cross-references in the MSA so auditors can see flow-down obligations without reviewing all vendor contracts.

Two asks for your redline: please add the narrow definition of "material risk" (see Priyom’s suggestion) and include the 5% credit in the Order Form as commercial consideration. Otherwise we can move to internal approvals on our side next week.

Maya
